analysis.one_liner: Abolishes OSHA, the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety rules.
analysis.headline: The bill to abolish the nation's workplace safety agency has sat without a single cosponsor in committee since its introduction, with no action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill repeals the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 and shuts down the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), the agency within the Department of Labor that writes and enforces workplace safety and health standards and runs related training and outreach. The result would be no federal inspector general-purpose safety standards, no federal workplace safety inspections, and no federal enforcement when employers expose workers to hazards. It was introduced with no cosponsors and referred to committee, where it has not moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, particularly those in hazardous industries like construction, meatpacking, warehousing, and manufacturing, gain by no longer facing federal safety inspections, citations, or penalties for unsafe conditions. Businesses that now spend money on OSHA compliance would save those costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 in its entirety and abolishes OSHA, removing the federal framework for workplace safety standards and enforcement.
With OSHA gone, employers would no longer face federal inspections, citations, or fines for unsafe working conditions, and would no longer bear the cost of complying with federal safety standards.

analysis.who_pays: Workers bear the risk. Without a federal agency setting safety standards or inspecting workplaces, employees in dangerous jobs would have no federal protection against unsafe machinery, toxic exposures, falls, or other hazards, and would absorb the injuries, illnesses, and deaths that federal enforcement currently works to prevent. Injured workers and their families would also lose the federal complaint channel for reporting unsafe conditions.

drawbacks.text: Abolishing OSHA would eliminate federal workplace safety and health standards, inspections, and enforcement, leaving workers with no federal agency to turn to when conditions are unsafe.
The bill offers no replacement: it simply repeals the 1970 act and abolishes the agency, so no state or private system would fill the gap nationwide.

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill is that OSHA's rules and penalties impose compliance costs on employers, especially small businesses, and that some standards are outdated or duplicative; abolishing the agency would end those costs. The honest answer is that those costs are the price of the enforcement that keeps workers safe, and the bill removes both the burden and the protection together.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls entirely on workers, who would lose the only federal system of workplace safety standards and enforcement, while the benefit is a cost saving for employers, some of it passed to consumers in lower prices and some kept as profit. Decades of workplace fatalities and injuries that federal standards and inspections address would become a matter of each employer's discretion. The trade is heavily one-sided.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on January 3, 2025, and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where no further action has been taken; it sits there with zero cosponsors while the Congress continues.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs of Arizona introduced the bill on January 3, 2025, the first day of the 119th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee has taken no further action on the bill, and no vote has occurred in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, workers are no worse off because the bill has not moved. Employers hoping to see OSHA abolished have gained nothing yet, but nothing has been lost either; the bill is dormant rather than defeated.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, so far, since nothing happened

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to abolish OSHA and referred it to committee as its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after receiving the referral, leaving it to die without a hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: House of Representatives
against.what_they_did: No member joined as a cosponsor, leaving the bill with zero support beyond its sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no vote or party split ever developed; its only support was its Republican sponsor.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking, warehousing)
industries.note: Abolishing OSHA would end federal safety inspections, citations, and penalties, letting these employers cut spending on safety compliance while shifting the risk of injury and death onto their workers. Workers' interest in safe conditions runs directly against the cost savings this bill offers employers.

Small employers would be relieved of OSHA compliance paperwork, training requirements, and the risk of fines, a genuine cost saving. But they would also lose OSHA's free on-site consultation and training assistance, and their workers would lose the same federal protections as everyone else.

industries.industry: Workplace safety equipment and consulting firms
industries.note: A market that exists largely to help employers comply with OSHA standards would shrink or disappear along with the standards. The loss to this industry tracks the loss of safety protection for workers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no cosponsors and no committee action more than a year and a half into the Congress, which is the typical path for a bill to die quietly at the end of the session. Absent a sudden wave of support, it will not receive a vote.
